title: Chief Ministers and criminality: 45% of India’s CMs have cases pending against them
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
45% (14) of India’s current Chief Ministers have criminal cases lodged against them, with Telangana’s Revanth Reddy topping the list, according to an analysis done by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR). Of the 89 cases lodged against Mr. Reddy, 72 are under serious sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) such as criminal intimidation, promoting enmity and assault, while 16 are others. The report, published on Monday (July 27, 2026), has analysed the self-sworn affidavits of CMs (from their last contested elections) of 31 States and Union territories.

Criminality of CMs

Following Mr. Reddy is West Bengal’s Suvendu Adhikari, who has 29 cases (39 charges of under serious IPC, 78 in others) and Karnataka’s D.K. Shivakumar with 19 cases (six under serious IPC sections, 45 in others). At the bottom of the list are Punjab’s Bhagwant Mann, Sikkim’s P.S. Tamang, Odisha’s Mohan Charan Majhi and Rajasthan’s Bhajan Lal Sharma with one case each. 11 of the 14 CMs with criminal cases against them have been booked under serious offences including bribery, criminal intimidation and in the case of Mr. Adhikari and Andhra Pradesh’s Chandrababu Naidu — attempt to murder. 

Also Read | About 30% of MPs and MLAs face serious criminal cases in India

Digging further into the top five CMs with the highest number of criminal cases against them, criminal intimidation is the most common grievous offence allegedly committed by them. In the case of Mr. Revanth Reddy, who has been elected thrice from Kodangal, the most grievous charge is one assault charge against a woman, followed by 34 charges of criminal intimidation and 22 counts of statements promoting community hatred. 

One charge of attempt to murder and two charges of sexual harassment are the most grievous charges against Mr. Adhikari. The TMC-turned-BJP politician, who has either been an MP or MLA since 2006, also has eight charges each of criminal intimidation and promoting enmity against him.  

In Karnataka, D.K. Shivakumar, who was been an MLA since 1989, has three charges of disappearance of evidence, and one charge each of bribery and forgery while Kerala CM V.D. Satheesan, who has represented Paravur since 2001, has three charges to deter a public servant from doing his duty, one count each under criminal intimidation, causing hurt by dangerous weapon. In Jharkhand, Hemant Soren, who has been an MLA since 2009, has one count each under forgery, cheating, theft etc. 

Tamil Nadu’s C Joseph Vijay, Mr. Majhi and Mr. Sharma remain the only exception with no serious offences lodged against them. While Mr. Vijay and Mr. Sharma are first time MLAs, Mr. Majhi has been elected four times to the Odisha Assembly from Keonjhar. 

Though NDA rules at least 22 States, only Mr. Adhikari features in the top five list of criminal CMs. Of the remaining four – Mr. Reddy, Mr. Shivakumar and Mr. Satheesan belong to Congress while Mr. Soren heads its ally Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM). 

Billionaire CMs

Richest CM in India is Mr. D.K Shivakumar with his total assets exceeding ₹1413 crores, followed by Mr. Naidu (₹931 crore), Mr. Vijay (₹648 crore) and Mr. Pema Khandu (₹332 crore). Among the low asset CMs are Jammu-Kashmir’s Omar Abdullah (₹55 lakh), Mr. Adhikari (₹85 lakhs) and Bhajan Lal Sharma (₹1 crore). 

A closer look at their declared assets shows Mr. Shivakumar ranking top in immovable assets (₹1140 crore), liabilities (₹265 crore) and disputed assets of ₹ 246 crore. On the other hand, Mr. Naidu tops the list in movable assets (₹810 crore), followed by Mr. Vijay (₹426 crore). The most common profession declared by these CMs are social/political work, agriculture and salary as a people’s representative. Exceptions to these are advocates – V.D. Satheesan (Kerala), Rekha Sharma (Delhi) and doctors Manik Saha (Tripura), Pramod Sawant (Goa). Inspite of achieving super stardom in Tamil Cinema, Mr. Vijay has declared his profession as a property owner and trustee.

Other attributes

Ms. Sharma has distinction as the lone female CM in India, making the gender bias skewed to 3%. In total, India has 390 female MLAs (9%) of the total 4123 representatives across state and UT assemblies, according to ADR. An agewise split of the 31 CMs show 17 between the ages 51-60, followed by 8 between 41-50. The oldest CMs falling between 71-80 years are – Andhra’s Mr. Naidu (74), Puducherry’s N Rangasamy (75), Mizoram’s Lalduhoma (73) and Nagaland’s Neiphiu Rio (72). Meghalaya’s Conrad Sangma and Arunachal Pradesh’s Pema Khandu are India’s youngest CMs at 44 years. 

Educational qualifications of the CMs show that 84% are atleast diploma or graduate holders, while two are 10th pass (Chhatisgarh’s Vishnu Deo Sai and Manipur’s Yumnam Khemchand Singh) and three are 12th pass (Mr. Vijay, Mr. Soren and Punjab’s Bhagwant Mann). Three CMs with the highest qualification - doctorate degree, are Madhya Pradesh’s Mohan Yadav, Asam’s Himanta Biswa Sarma and Bihar’s Samrat Choudhary. The CMs with the least and the highest educational qualifications all belong to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

title: CBI files charge sheet against 13 accused in NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has filed a charge sheet against 13 arrested accused persons in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case, the agency said on Tuesday (July 28, 2026). All of them are currently in judicial custody.

The charge sheet comes days after Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned from the post on July 25, in the wake of over a month-long agitation led by the Cockroach Janta Party.

The agency has invoked provisions related to criminal conspiracy, cheating, criminal breach of trust, destruction of evidence and other associated charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act.

It has cited 360 witnesses, 422 documents, and 43 material objects in the charge sheet.

The agency registered the case based on a complaint lodged by the Department of Higher Education on May 12, alleging irregularities in the conduct of the NEET-UG 2026 examination, which was held on May 3. The test was subsequently cancelled.

The CBI formed multiple teams with 72 officials and personnel, along with eight cyber forensic experts, to investigate the case. Searches were carried out at 92 locations in Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, and other States.

“These searches led to the seizure of incriminating material like digital and communication devices, documents etc. Forensic imaging and analysis of the incriminating material has been undertaken,” said the agency, adding that source of the leak was unearthed within weeks.

“The path from source of the leak to the beneficiary candidates was unearthed, leading to the identification of the chain. The first arrest in this case was made on May 13, 2026, it said.

Among the arrested are three National Testing Agency (NTA) subject experts in chemistry (P.V. Kulkarni), biology (Manisha Gurunath Mandhare), and physics (Manisha Sanjay Havaldar).

Another key accused is Shivaraj Motegaonkar, a professor and owner of RCC Coaching Institute in Maharashtra’s Latur.

Several alleged intermediaries who sourced and distributed the leaked questions were also held. Tejas Harshadkumar Shah, physics faculty and chief operating officer at APMA Coaching Institute, Pune, was also arrested.

“Digital forensic analysis reports, handwriting expert opinions and academic experts’ opinions regarding leaked questions have been obtained. These reports confirmed the role of the accused in the circulation of leaked questions before the date of examination,” said the CBI. Further investigation is under way.

title: Rajnath Singh unveils Coast Guard reforms to boost gender equality
author: Saurabh Trivedi
content_html:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday (July 28, 2026) unveiled two major policy reforms for the Indian Coast Guard (ICG), introducing a gender-neutral framework for the induction and career progression of officers and simplifying the process of granting ex gratia compensation to the families of personnel reported missing at sea while on duty.

The reforms were announced at an event held at Kartavya Bhavan-2 in New Delhi, attended by Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, Director General, Indian Coast Guard, Paramesh Sivamani and other senior officials.

The Ministry of Defence described the measures as forward-looking reforms. Mr Singh said they would strengthen the force's morale and operational effectiveness as it prepares to celebrate its Swarnim Jayanti (Golden Jubilee) in 2027. He reiterated the government’s commitment to building a modern, capable and future-ready Coast Guard under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The first policy introduces a comprehensive gender-neutral framework for officer induction. It allows women to be inducted through both Short Service Appointment (SSA) and Permanent Appointment (PA) streams on par with their male counterparts, while opening the SSA entry route for male candidates as well.

Equal opportunities

The policy also ensures equal opportunities for career progression from the initial training stage. Existing women officers holding Permanent Appointments will be eligible for promotion to higher ranks subject to prescribed conditions, while serving women officers under the SSA scheme will have the option to convert to Permanent Appointment after meeting the stipulated eligibility criteria.

The Defence Ministry said the reform reflected the government’s commitment to promoting Nari Shakti and ensuring equal opportunities within India’s maritime security framework.

The second reform aims to provide timely financial relief to the next of kin of Coast Guard personnel who go missing at sea while performing their duties. Under the new policy, the competent authority will be empowered to declare such personnel as “presumed dead” solely for the purpose of processing ex-gratia compensation and terminal benefits.

The Ministry said the revised procedure would significantly reduce administrative delays, enabling bereaved families to receive financial assistance and service benefits without prolonged waiting periods during times of distress.

title: Study cites Soligas of Biligiri as an example against ‘fortress conservation approach’
author: K.C. Deepika
content_html:
Recommendations
Establishing a collaborative group including interested representatives from the Forest Department, Soliga elders, and researchers.
Recognising Soliga’s knowledge and skills to manage the landscape while understanding the importance of cultural rituals and ceremonies through which they learn and express gratitude towards nature.
Developing co-governance and co-management models, befitting local rules and regulations and the cultural context.
Building people’s capabilities to use modern techniques, such as GIS, for mapping sacred and cultural sites and other areas of importance for resource collection, as well as for monitoring, evaluation, and landscape management.
Developing reliable, sustainable, equitable, culturally appropriate incentivising mechanisms involving minimum transactional costs possible, in consultation with Soligas.

Wildlife conservation is typically achieved by excluding, evacuating or alienating the rights of indigenous people and local communities. A new research article published in the journal Ecosystems and People said this “fortress conservation approach” has led to uprooting, ongoing distress and despondency worldwide, and offers the Soligas in the Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple Wildlife Sanctuary (BRTWS) as a prime conservation exemplar, where tribal people have been living with wild animals, especially tigers, leopards, elephants and managing forest resources for millennia.

It highlighted the need to understand and recognise the importance of Adivasi people’s connections, knowledge and skills in forest management.

The article, ‘Fortress conservation versus traditional forest management: The example of Soliga tribal people from the Western Ghats, India’ authored by Kamaljit K. Sanghaa, M. Balasubramanian, C. Madegowda, Siddappa Setty and Jeremy Russell-Smitha from Research Institute for the Environment and Livelihoods, Charles Darwin University, Darwin, Australia; Centre for Ecological Economics and Natural Resources, Institute for Social and Economic Change, Bengaluru; and Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment, Bengaluru, was published on Monday, July 27.

Engagement over years

The researchers engaged formally and informally with Soliga elders to co-develop insights and solutions for both conservation and community needs through two workshops between 2022 and 2023, in addition to one-on-one talks with key elders in the community during their visits to the B.R. Hills since 2017.

Throughout the Western Ghats, Adivasi people and many local communities (approximately 5,000,000 Adivasi people just in Kerala and Karnataka as per 2011 Census data) have well-established, imbued relationships with the landscape, the researchers pointed out in the article.

Traditionally, the article said, Soligas managed the Biligiri area applying mosaic litter burning and small-scale swidden agriculture, without having to deal with noxious invasive weeds such as L. camara. People used to clear land for two to three years of cultivation, which subsequently enabled the colonisation of palatable grasses that served as food resources for various herbivores and, consequently, carnivores, especially tigers.

“The management of forests and related revered sacred and cultural values is integral to the Soligas’ way of life. They have hundreds of sacred and cultural places embedded within the Biligiri landscape with which people hold ongoing relationships through various customs, cultural practices, ceremonies and norms. Such an integrated coexistence of Soligas with the Biligiri landscape challenges prevailing conservation approaches, which typically rely on principles of human exclusion,” it said.

The article also noted that during workshops and informal conversations, Soliga elders expressed their aspirations to contribute to sustainable forest management outcomes.

“For example, Soligas have well-established local ‘podu’ level committees called ‘Sangha’ which are further grouped into ‘Taluka Sangha’, bringing all Soligas men and women together for decision-making. They have collectively prepared culturally relevant management plans with help from local NGOs that can be discussed with Forest Department authorities. On occasion, Soligas are asked to assist in managing wildfires, applying culturally relevant knowledge and skills. A few get the opportunity to work casually as forest guards,” it said.

Living with the wild

Occasionally, accidents involving wildlife are reported in the Biligiri hills, including annual encounters with tigers or elephants and leopard attacks on livestock. However, one of the perspectives cited in the article said, “We’ve been living with tigers for centuries. We know tiger and elephant behaviour, and they know ours. We know their smell and sound, and we do not go to those places. Many birds ring alarm bells, so we move to different areas. Monkeys and langurs give call sounds. These are life skills. We look after the forest and leave some things for the animals; for example, we do not take all the honey, we leave some for the animals. We worship the tiger, elephant and bison.”

“Involving tribal people with the knowledge and skills to manage their natural systems can offer a win-win situation for supporting people’s well-being and for governments to reduce management costs and protect wildlife in Protected Areas. The BRTWS example demonstrates the cost-effective practical advantages of a collaborative, community-based conservation approach for meeting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and ensuring the delivery of ecosystem services for local communities and wider society,” the researchers said.

We know their smell and sound, and we do not go to those places. Many birds ring alarm bells, so we move to different areas. Monkeys and langurs give call sounds. These are life skills. We look after the forest and leave some things for the animals; for example, we do not take all the honey, we leave some for the animals. We worship the tiger, elephant and bison.”
“Involving tribal people with the knowledge and skills to manage their natural systems can offer a win-win situation for supporting people’s well-being and for governments to reduce management costs and protect wildlife in Protected Areas. The BRTWS example demonstrates the cost-effective practical advantages of a collaborative, community-based conservation approach for meeting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and ensuring the delivery of ecosystem services for local communities and wider society,” the researchers said.

title: Bengaluru: Namma Metro recorded 59 track-related incidents since 2012
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Bengaluru metro has recorded 59 track-related incidents over the past 14 years, including suicide attempts, suicide deaths, accidental falls and unauthorised track access, according to data from the Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. (BMRCL).

The figures, covering the period from 2012 to 2025, have come under renewed focus following the death of a passenger who allegedly jumped in front of an approaching train at Huskur Road Metro Station on the Yellow Line on Monday, once again intensifying demands for platform screen doors (PSDs) across the network.

The BMRCL data shows that 31 cases involved unauthorised track access, 16 were suicide attempts, eight were passengers falling onto the tracks, and four resulted in suicide deaths.

Past incidents

The first such incident on the Namma Metro network was recorded in 2012, when a 16-year-old first-year student allegedly jumped in front of an approaching train at M.G. Road Metro Station at around 8.35 p.m.

The number of incidents has risen over the years as the Metro network has expanded and daily ridership has increased.

Suicide attempts reached their highest level in 2024, when eight cases were reported. The number fell to five in 2025, while two attempts were recorded in 2021 and one in 2019. Suicide deaths were reported once in 2012, twice in 2024 and once in 2025.

Accidental falls onto the tracks were relatively few in the early years but increased to three cases in 2022, followed by two each in 2024 and 2025.

Unauthorised track access accounted for more than half of all incidents. Such cases increased from four in 2021 to six in 2022, peaked at eight in 2023, before declining slightly to seven in 2024 and five in 2025.

While in 2026, according to officials two suicide-related incidents have already been reported in July this year, including Monday’s fatal incident at Huskur Road Metro Station.

The Huskur incident follows several similar tragedies on the Bengaluru Metro network in recent years. On December 5, 2025, a 38-year-old engineer died by suicide after jumping in front of a Purple Line train at Kengeri Metro Station. Earlier, on August 3, 2024, a 57-year-old man died after jumping before a Green Line train at Doddakallasandra Metro Station. On March 21, 2024, a 19-year-old law student died after jumping onto the Purple Line tracks at Attiguppe Metro Station.

Platform screen doors

The latest death has once again revived the long-standing demand for the installation of platform screen doors, which create a physical barrier between passengers and the tracks and open only when trains arrive.

However, BMRCL has no immediate plans to install PSDs across its 96-km operational Metro network. Officials have maintained that retrofitting existing stations with platform screen doors is technically challenging as it would require extensive structural modifications, integration with signalling systems and precise alignment with train doors.

An official said, “It would be technically challenging and the cost of upgrading all operational stations is substantial and is therefore not being considered at present.”

Instead, BMRCL has introduced steel safety barricades at several high-footfall stations, including Majestic Interchange, M.G. Road, Indiranagar, Benniganahalli and RV Road, to discourage passengers from entering the track area while allowing safe boarding and alighting.

Looking ahead, the Metro corporation has proposed installing platform screen doors at 177 stations, including existing operational stations, as part of the Detailed Project Report for the proposed Hebbal–Sarjapur Metro corridor (Phase 3A). The proposal is currently awaiting approval from the Union Government.

(If you are in distress or having suicidal tendencies, please reach out to these helplines: TeleMANAS at 1-8008914416/ 14416, NIMHANS at 08026685948, 9480829670 or SAHAI at 080 25497777, +91-9886444075)

title: CJP solidarity protest in Chennai’s Balan Illam keeps alive the legacy of Communist leader Baladhandayutham
author: B. Kolappan
content_html:
No venue could have been more appropriate than Balan Illam, the headquarters of the Communist Party of India (CPI) located in Chennai, for the recent protest in solidarity with the Cockroach Janta (CJP) Party and against NEET in Tamil Nadu.

Balan was the popular name of K. Baladhandayutham, a towering CPI leader who began his political career as a student activist. He was expelled from Annamalai University in 1938 for his political activities. His life was, in many ways, quixotic, marked by an unwavering commitment to communist ideals. He was only 20 when his university education came to an abrupt end, after which he plunged into full-time politics.

The protests against NEET continued at Balan Illam, the office of the CPI in Chennai. File | Photo Credit: Bijoy Ghosh

The Vice-Chancellor of the university at the time was the Right Honourable V.S. Srinivasa Sastri. Baladhandayutham famously quipped: “He is neither right nor honourable.”

A year after his expulsion, he married his classmate, Claudius Wills, an Anglo-Indian. However, barely six months into their marriage, he was arrested. After serving a one-year prison sentence, he was re-arrested at the gates of Coimbatore Prison and spent another 18 months in Vellore Central Prison.

Claudius Wills, whom Balan renamed Nirmala, hoped he would abandon political activism and pursue another career. He refused. Recalling the episode in a letter to his fellow communist Balraj, Balan wrote: “She waited for me for 12 years. But it was of no use. She obtained a divorce in 1951 and remarried. Her remarriage gave me immense joy.”

A gifted orator and writer, Balan spent several years underground after the Communist Party was banned. He was later sentenced to life imprisonment in the Nellai Conspiracy Case, in which veteran communist leaders R. Nallakannu and P. Manickam also received long prison terms. Registered in 1949, the case named Balan as the first accused. His experiences as a life convict were serialised in Samaran magazine and later published as the book Yen Aayul Thandanai Anubhavangal.

K. Baladhandayutham (artistic sketch) Photo credit: Special arrangement

Balan was only 55 when he was killed in an air crash alongside Mohan Kumaramangalam, the communist-turned-Congress leader and Union Minister. In his lifetime, he spent more than 16 years in prison and several more living underground. When the Communist Party split in 1964, he remained with the CPI. At the time of his death in 1973, he was the Lok Sabha member representing the Coimbatore constituency.

Reflecting on the purpose of his life’s struggles, Baladhandayutham wrote to Balraj: “If a young person reads or hears my story and dedicates his life to the service of the nation, I will have the satisfaction that I have not wasted my life.”

One of those inspired by Balan was the renowned Tamil writer Jayakanthan, who rejoined the Communist Party after listening to Baladhandayutham speak at Chintadripet in Madras following his release from prison.

“He spoke for two hours. It was not merely a speech; it was as though Bharathi and Tilak had come together in the form of a lion and roared. Standing amidst the crowd, I lost all awareness of myself and listened with the conviction that he was my leader. As Balan stood on the dais, he seemed, on the one hand, to resemble Bharathi and, on the other, Bhagat Singh,” Mr. Jayakanthan wrote in Oru Ilakkiyavathiyin Arasiyal Anubhavangal.

Mr. Jayakanthan writes that Baladhandayutham was a hero to educated youth and communists alike. His daring exploits, powerful oratory and personal sacrifices were recounted almost as legends, he says.

Born into a wealthy agricultural family at Makkinanpatti near Pollachi, Balan recalled in his letter to Balraj that he organised a children’s union and led protests against toddy shops and textile merchants selling foreign cloth. “Our heads were not broken and we were not sent to jail because we were children,” he wrote. While still in high school, he founded the Radical Youth Club, which served as a political training ground.

After his expulsion from the university and release from prison, Balan worked among railway workers at Ponmalai. In 1945, the party sent him to Tirunelveli to build its organisation. He went underground in 1946 after a warrant was issued for his arrest in the wake of the railway strike.

“In 1948, I attended the Party Congress in Calcutta. A warrant was issued for my arrest again, forcing me to go underground. I remained underground for five years,” Balan recalled in his memoirs.

He was arrested in 1949 in the Nellai Conspiracy Case on charges that the communists had conspired to overthrow the Nehru government. After the judgment was delivered in 1953, he was brutally assaulted inside the police van while being taken to prison.

“They abused me. They punched me. They rolled me on the floor and hurled me into the lorry. After chaining my hands, they felt victorious. Their hatred suffocated me,” he wrote.

While lodged in Madurai Prison, Balan undertook a fast unto death along with 13 other communists convicted in the case. He was subsequently shifted to Madras, then to Nagpur, before finally being brought back to Tamil Nadu.

Even in prison, Balan remained intellectually active. He started a handwritten magazine called Thudaippam (Broomstick). The “magazine” consisted of a display board on which prisoners pinned their writings for others to read.

“I learnt wrestling in prison. But I could not persevere for long. I even became the subject of a caricature in the magazine,” he recalled with characteristic humour.

Balan was also a regular contributor to the party organ Janasakthi and its literary magazine Thamarai. He once wrote that he could not continue watching the film Kappalottiya Thamizhan, based on the life of V.O. Chidambaram, because tears prevented him from remaining in the theatre.

Nellai S. Velayutham, a senior communist leader and one of Balan’s close associates, recalled the words Balan uttered after his release from prison: “I was born a full-time worker, and I will die a full-time worker.”

He lived true to those words.

title: State Highways expedites work on ₹24-crore high-level bridge across Then Pennar river in Tiruvannamalai
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The State Highways has expedited the ongoing work of the new ₹24-crore high-level bridge across Then Pennar river between Agarampallipattu and Thondamanur villages near Thandrampattu town in Tiruvannamalai, bringing relief to hundreds of residents in the surrounding 20 farming villages.

Officials of State Highways, which executes the multi-crore work, said that the new bridge is a replacement for the bridge, that was washed away after the Water Resources Department (WRD) released excess rainwater of over two lakh cusecs from Sathanur dam due to heavy rain triggered by Cyclone Fengal in December 2024.

“The design of the new bridge has been completely revised based on the existing water course of the river. The new facility will be ready by December 2026 for public use,” S. Dinesh, Assistant Engineer (AE), State Highways (Tiruvannamalai), told The Hindu.

Highways officials said that the collapsed bridge, that was opened for public use in September 2024, collapsed three months later.

On the contrary, the new bridge is being built 300 metres away from the earlier spot across the river to ensure the facility remains aligned with the river. It gives more durability to the structure. “Also, the total height of the new bridge has been increased to 10 metres from the riverbed as against four metres for the earlier bridge. The increased height helps prevent inundation of the carriageway of the bridge,” Mr. Dinesh said.

Funded under the Comprehensive Road Infrastructure Development Programme (CRIDP) 2024-25, the new bridge will be 356-metre-long and 12-metres-wide - sufficient for two buses to ply at any given time. It will have tiled footpaths, LED lights, inlets to discharge rainwater into the river, reflectors, sign boards, and hand railings. Approach roads will be laid to connect surrounding villages with the new facility.

“The new bridge should be completed before the Northeast monsoon because it will help the village get ambulance services in a short time. The new facility will also help restore bus services in villages in the area,” said D. Pulivendan, president, Thondamanur village panchayat,

For residents, the new bridges will end a detour of at least 30 km to reach nearest towns like Polur, Arani, Chengam, and Tiruvannamalai.
